At PraisonAI 4.6.31, the original tool-loading trigger is blocked while the tool_override path still violates the invariant. This reproduces the publicly documented CVE-2026-44334 bypass of CVE-2026-40287; neither tested path shows a violation at 4.6.32. For CrewAI, we observe a violation in tested release 1.11.0 and confinement in 1.11.1, without claiming the earliest fixed release. Fourteen harness-validation scenarios produced their expected verdicts.

The PraisonAI probes invoke loader functions directly and establish boundary behavior under the supplied setup, not a full end-to-end exploit. title: Replay-Augmented Regularisation for Class-Incremental Network Intrusion Detection: A Three-Dataset Evaluation of EWC and LwF
summary: As new attack categories emerge, network intrusion detection models need to be updated; however, when fine-tuned sequentially on new classes, previous classes are forgotten, resulting in catastrophic for- getting. The three public datasets we use are UNSW-NB15, ToN-IoT and CIC-IDS2017, and for these datasets, our class-incremental intrusion detection system is built using a CNN with one-dimensional (1D) archi- tecture trained over nine sequential tasks, each of which introduces one attack category. We evaluate sequential fine-tuning without any buffe compared to Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and Learning without Forgetting (LwF), both of which include a class-size-adaptive rehearsal buffer of 20% of all previous classes (from 20 to 300 samples). The hyper-parameters were selected using UNSW-NB15 and fixed for the other two datasets. On UNSW-NB15, replay improves the final accuracy of both regularisers to 73.6% (EWC) and 71.1% (LwF) compared to about 32% (no improvement over fine-tuning). LwF with replay achieves 46.1% and 91.6% final accuracy for the two frozen-configuration datasets (ToN-IoT, CIC-IDS2017) while EWC with replay achieves 23.7% and 61.9%. In order to avoid this, EWC was therefore tuned on one dataset and the other two data sets were used as test sets. It is also demonstrated that the common forgetting measure can be misleading for a model which does not learn the old classes. As the fine-tuning baseline was not re- played and all the results were based on a single seed, it is not claimed hat the regularisers provide any extra support over replay alone.

Paper:
title: Beyond Semantic Prompts: Unified Watermarking and Access Control for Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion services require both traceability of generated content and differentiated access to generation capabilities. However, existing watermarking methods commonly expose watermark control through mechanisms beyond the text-prompt interface, while credential-based access control does not inherently enforce distinct output quality levels. We propose a unified framework that enables customizable multi-bit watermark embedding and tiered access control through a single text prompt. A unified prompt represents watermark messages using designated words and associates protocol structures with different access states. The framework adopts a two-stage training strategy. First, watermark payload partitioning represents messages as designated watermark words, while vocabulary extension assigns each protocol word a dedicated token with a learnable input embedding. Guided by a frozen reference model and a pretrained watermark codec, joint adaptation of the U-Net and protocol-token embeddings transfers message-dependent watermark patterns into the generation process. Second, a prompt-structure recognition network controls feature modulation within the variational autoencoder decoder, which is trained to produce clear watermarked images, blurred previews, or black outputs according to the access state. Experiments demonstrate reliable watermark recovery, robustness to common image-processing operations and evaluated model modifications, and consistent performance across diverse generation settings. The controlled decoder also achieves distinct output behaviors under restricted access while closely preserving reference decoding fidelity and watermark recoverability under full access. Our open-source code and model weights will be public after acceptance.

Paper:
title: Designing Deceptive Model Organisms that Successfully Evade Auditing
summary: AI models can exhibit deceptive behaviors such as strategically underperforming on evaluations (sandbagging), faking alignment, or covertly acting on behalf of a hidden principal. Safe deployment therefore requires auditing techniques that can reliably detect such behaviors. To develop and test these techniques, we can train model organisms (MOs): models that exhibit deceptive behaviors and serve as realistic evaluation testbeds. However, for such testbeds to be informative, MOs must actively anticipate and resist auditing---a gap in prior work that can lead to overestimation of auditing effectiveness and underestimation of safety risks. We address this gap by designing MOs that capture worst-case deceptive behavior and evade high-effort auditing. Focusing on sandbagging, we frame MO design as a security game between an auditor and a deceptive model and identify three design requirements for sandbagging MOs: (i) effectiveness (underperforming on targeted capabilities), (ii) utility preservation (maintaining performance on all other capabilities), and (iii) robustness (resisting auditing). We propose three MOs: two optimized against blackbox auditing techniques and one optimized against both blackbox and whitebox techniques. Through a comprehensive evaluation, we show that, unlike MOs from prior work, our MOs satisfy all three requirements, providing worst-case baselines for developing and evaluating future auditing techniques.

Paper:
title: KVMARK: Fragile Watermarking for KV-Cache Integrity in Latent Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Latent multi-agent communication directly transfers Key-Value (KV) cache tensors between transformer-based agents, bypassing text serialization entirely. While computationally efficient and reasoning accurate, this communication channel is opaque and vulnerable to man-in-the-middle tampering, a threat vector unaddressed by existing text-based or behavioral watermarks, which cannot operate on continuous internal representations. To address this vulnerability, we propose KVMark, a training-free, zero-bit KV-cache watermarking framework to verify inter-agent handoff integrity. Our framework introduces four core technical components: (1) position-dependent sign patterns that guarantee first-order statistical invisibility while preserving downstream attention survival; (2) per-head sign patterns with aligned detection to defeat head-averaging attacks; (3) a three-tier depth-aware strength schedule that equalizes detection sensitivity across transformer layers while maintaining invisibility against nine statistical profiling strategies; and (4) content-bound key derivation that cryptographically binds watermarks to input contexts, preventing replay attacks under Kerckhoffs's principle. Empirical evaluation on a four-agent latent pipeline demonstrates $100\%$ detection across $1{,}500$ handoffs with a $0.0\%$ false positive rate ($\text{AUROC}=1.0$), $100\%$ layer-level tamper localization ($17/17$ attacked layers identified with $0/19$ false positives), and no statistically significant reasoning accuracy degradation across four benchmarks ($N{=}300$--$500$). Furthermore, the framework enables multi-hop cascade verification to isolate compromised agents (500/500 detection at three hops), withstands adaptive white-box adversaries and the Out-of-Sight DiffMean attack (up to $α=8.0$), and generalizes seamlessly to Qwen3-8B without re-tuning (1,500/1,500 TPR).

Paper:
title: Taint Analysis via Heap-Aware Propagation
summary: Taint analysis for C depends on how precisely the analysis tracks tainted values as they flow through memory objects. Without field sensitivity, a tainted object field can spuriously taint an entire object, producing significant false alarms. In this paper, we present a field-sensitive taint analysis that combines Data Structure Analysis (DSA) for field-sensitive points-to information with a data-flow analysis for tracking explicit dependencies. We identify that existing DSA-style analyses lose precision on a common object pattern: a C struct object that mixes scalar fields with a flexible array member. When such an array is accessed with symbolic indices, DSA loses points-to field sensitivity for the entire object, inflating false alarms in the data-flow analysis.
  To address this, we propose I-DSA, which extends DSA by representing field positions as intervals, so that a pointer with symbolic bounds merges only the fields within those bounds. We further develop a sound data-flow analysis based on abstract interpretation. We implement I-DSA on top of SeaDSA and the data-flow analysis inside Crab. Our tool targets LLVM IR and supports configurable taint policies by instrumenting the IR with taint intrinsics. Our experiments show that I-DSA reduces the false alarms caused by this pattern at little cost in the pointer analysis, that SVF, an inclusion-based pointer analysis, shows a similar field-sensitivity loss, and that our taint analysis scales better than PhASAR on real-world programs.

Paper:
title: Self-organizing recruitment cascades couple Levy search to a clustered maximum-entropy resource field
summary: Foraging recruitment is modeled as a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade on the group's communication network. Because activation is degree-normalized, crowding shuts the cascade off, causing the swarm to aggregate on a resource and then disperse to explore again. Acting on the cascade moves agents in space, rewiring the network; recruitment and exploration are thus one coupled process, and removing this coupling alone abolishes self-limitation. Recruitment spreads only within a connectivity window bounded below by percolation onset and above by degree-blocking. The swarm self-organizes to the near-critical edge of this window--self-organized quasi-criticality--hovering near but below the critical point without settling onto a size-invariant critical state, with a finite-correlation-time activity spectrum (Lorentzian-like, not 1/f) consistent with local criticality. Recruitment raises harvest up to 2.7x over solitary search on sparse, clustered fields and loses (down to 0.37x) on abundant or uniform ones; because resources generically aggregate, the favourable regime is the common one. The Levy search and resource field are both least-committal: a maximum-caliber walk coupled to a maximum-entropy point process whose generic sign is clustered, with the optimal search exponent tracking the field's fractal dimension. Heavy-tailed Levy exploration crosses sparse voids while recruitment cascades exploit clusters by switching agents to short local steps, binding exploration and recruitment into a single self-organizing cycle.

Paper:
title: Where the Evidence Lives: Measuring Privacy and Diagnosability of Exported AI-Agent Traces
summary: Execution traces help diagnose AI-agent failures, but sharing them can expose customer identities. For example, detecting that an agent handled the wrong customer's records requires knowing whether the records belong to the requested customer, but not necessarily knowing who that customer is. Our executable benchmark measures what a trace export reveals and whether a proposed repair restores the correct output in synthetic multi-tenant workflows. Conventional redaction can remove evidence needed for repair while leaving encoded identifiers recoverable. Two exports preserve ownership comparisons by reporting the match as a comparison fact or by using pseudonyms consistent within each execution. Both preserve the original diagnostic program's repairs. The tested identifier matchers identify no requested customer from either export. An independently written program produces correct outputs on 39 of 42 faulty cases with comparison facts and on all 42 with execution-scoped pseudonyms. Row counts still expose identities. With prior knowledge of customers' row counts, an attacker uniquely identifies the requested customer in 97 of 240 executions under each of the 15 export policies. Removing selected counters from the comparison-fact export stops this attack and preserves the original program's repairs. The benchmark lets engineers test what their diagnostic program can repair and what an attacker can still infer from the same export.

Paper:
title: A Comprehensive Survey on Orbital Edge Computing: Systems, Applications, and Algorithms
summary: The number of satellites, especially those operating in low-earth orbit (LEO), is exploding in recent years. Additionally, the use of COTS hardware into those satellites enables a new paradigm of computing: orbital edge computing (OEC). OEC entails more technically advanced steps compared to single-satellite computing. This feature allows for vast design spaces with multiple parameters, rendering several novel approaches feasible. The mobility of LEO satellites in the network and limited resources of communication, computation, and storage make it challenging to design an appropriate scheduling algorithm for specific tasks in comparison to traditional ground-based edge computing. This article comprehensively surveys the significant areas of focus in orbital edge computing, which include protocol optimization, mobility management, and resource allocation. This article provides the first comprehensive survey of OEC. Previous survey papers have only concentrated on ground-based edge computing or the integration of space and ground technologies. This article presents a review of recent research from 2000 to 2023 on orbital edge computing that covers network design, computation offloading, resource allocation, performance analysis, and optimization. Moreover, having discussed several related works, both technological challenges and future directions are highlighted in the field.

title: Beyond Service Discovery: Coverage Awareness in LLM-Driven Service Composition
summary: Large language models increasingly support the automated discovery and composition of services. In federated data ecosystems, this creates new opportunities for reusing existing data products and transformation services when constructing service-based data exchange modeled as data-sharing pipelines. However, finding relevant reusable assets does not imply that the available assets are sufficient to satisfy a consumer request. In this paper, we distinguish reuse discovery, the ability to identify relevant published assets, from reuse coverage, the extent to which the available assets support the transformations required by a request. We further consider coverage awareness, the ability of a composition system to recognize insufficient coverage. We investigate this distinction using PipeFinder, an LLM-driven framework for composing data-sharing pipelines, and evaluate 99 consumer requests against a fixed catalogue of data products and transformation services. Our experiments show that relevant data products can be discovered reliably, while successful composition remains considerably more difficult. More importantly, when required transformation services are missing, the framework typically constructs a pipeline from the available services rather than recognizing that the request cannot be satisfied. Explicitly incorporating coverage checking into the planning procedure substantially improves recognition of such cases. These results suggest that coverage awareness should be treated as an explicit concern in LLM-driven service composition and cannot be assumed to follow from improved discovery or model capability.
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20333v1

Paper:
title: AutoCedar: An Agentic Framework for Verifier-Guided Access Control Policy Synthesis
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly used to turn natural-language requirements into code. In access control, that shortcut is dangerous: a generated policy can compile and read correctly while granting access that no one approved. The difficulty is not only writing policy code. It is fixing what the requirements mean before code is written, and then checking that the final policy actually satisfies that intent. We present AutoCedar, a verifier-guided system that first turns natural-language access-control requirements into a reviewed, checkable target, and then synthesizes Cedar policies against that target. AutoCedar decomposes schema and policy authoring into small intent atoms: reviewable claims about vocabulary and behavior. Once those atoms pass mechanical validation and human intent review, the model proposes a candidate policy, the verifier checks it against the approved target, and each failure is turned into a repair signal that tells the model whether to broaden, narrow, or restructure the policy without changing the target. Because the model's work is split into small problems, each grounded in reviewed intent and backed by verifier feedback, end-to-end policy authoring becomes tractable. AutoCedar converges on all 221 tasks of CedarBench, our benchmark of authorization tasks paired with executable semantic boundaries. Across three requirements-corpus case studies covering healthcare, education, and conference management, AutoCedar converts noisy prose and extracted access-control fragments into reviewed schemas, formal checks, and a globally verified Cedar policy store for each scenario.

Paper:
title: Reconstructing False Alarm and Detection Rates in Quantum Machine Learning for Intrusion Detection
summary: Published results in quantum machine learning for intrusion detection (QML-IDS) require joint interpretation of false-positive rate (FPR), attack true-positive rate (TPR), and evaluation provenance. We reconstruct operating points in the 25-entry frame selected by Kaissar and colleagues: 21 included articles, 20 identified documentary families, substantive methodological material consulted for 15, and 24 descriptive points from five. In one test-labelled comparison, a quantum support vector machine reduces FPR from 6.875% for random forest to 3.329%, while TPR decreases from 93.955% to 93.682%; both rates improve against three other comparators. In another study, a complete benign row identifies FPR as 12/6000 (0.200%), despite incomplete attack-side allocation that requires additional assumptions for TPR. Normalized matrices identify detection ranges rather than a unique aggregate rate. A uniform provenance rule separates training-described and test-adjusted results from six conditional illustrations whose independence remains unverified. The contribution is a reproducible interpretation of favorable comparisons and detection trade-offs, without converting descriptive results or hypothetical calculations into operational guarantees.

Paper:
title: Type-Confusion Security
summary: Type systems are a lightweight way to obtain formal assurance that code upholds security properties. However, decentralized systems, such as smart contracts and Model Context Protocol ecosystems, have limited ability to constrain the behavior of untrusted code. In such systems, attackers may attempt to confuse trusted code by supplying values that do not behave according to their advertised types, an attack that we call type confusion. Well-known attacks such as confused deputy attacks, reentrancy attacks, and control-flow hijacking can be understood as instances of type confusion. We define type confusion security as the property that unrestricted attackers who need not follow the type system have no more power than limited attackers who fully obey it. We formally define type confusion security as a real--ideal emulation, and in the context of an information-flow-typed core calculus that statically enforces security against well-typed attackers, prove that its run-time checks also enforce security against ill-typed attackers. In this system, programmers can write code while reasoning about security only against well-typed attackers; the security guarantees enforced by the type system still hold. We mechanize a proof of type confusion security in Lean.

Paper:
title: Clawdrain: Exploiting Tool-Calling Chains for Stealthy Token Exhaustion in OpenClaw Agents
summary: Tool-calling LLM agents rely on third-party skills to extend their capabilities, but this openness exposes a supply-chain attack surface in which malicious skill instructions can manipulate agent execution across multiple turns. In this work, we present Clawdrain, a Trojanized OpenClaw skill that induces resource exhaustion through a Segmented Verification Process (SVP). SVP combines stateful progression, repair-driven repetition, and termination to create costly tool-calling chains while preserving a legitimate final payload. We evaluate Clawdrain in a production-like OpenClaw deployment with real API billing across Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Clawdrain achieves 2-16 times token amplification with plain SVP, while the three models exhibit distinct behaviors, including autoregressive compliance, proactive scripting, and extended trial-and-error reasoning. Our findings reveal that agent resource exhaustion arises not only from output generation, but also from repeated context re-ingestion, tool coordination, reasoning, and recovery, motivating system-level controls over cumulative skill behavior.

Paper:
title: Where the Savings Go: The Limits of Hiding Cross-Tenant Cache Hits in LLM Serving
summary: LLM serving engines cache prompt prefixes; a cache hit skips computation and returns faster, so a shared cache reveals whether others have sent a given text. Per-account salting closes this channel but forgoes cross-tenant reuse and isolates only whole accounts, even where access is redistributed or trust domains are subdivided below them. Defenses that share globally but hide hits promise reuse without relying on account boundaries. Hiding a hit requires everything tenants observe afterwards to be distributed as if it had missed. The defenses we examine target the hit-miss gap; we instead follow where the saved time goes. Step-based schedulers that never idle while work waits pass it in full to every request queued behind the hit, shifting each earlier by the same amount. An attacker within ordinary rate limits brackets a probe with two groups of listeners that each return one token, sends them in one short burst, and counts in how many steps they finish. Replaying a production trace on one vLLM instance at up to half capacity, a single probe detects cached texts of 256 tokens or more with advantage at least 0.98. Hiding only the hit request falls to one probe on vLLM and SGLang; random delays must reach about ten times the shift or more to cut the advantage to 0.1; narrowing what is shared gives no guarantee against this inference. Since any observable tenant benefit is also a signal, we prove that a rate-limited tenant's gain from content written by k other accounts is at most of order k times the leakage allowed, whatever the provider does with identities; at zero leakage, only the provider keeps the savings. Exact hiding is attainable in principle on one instance, but mechanisms that only pause or hold work know skipped work's duration only approximately, so under saturated prefill they must pad every step that may hold a hit, at a price that grows with time rather than with hits.

Paper:
title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
summary: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration. TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met. For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16. NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.

Paper:
title: A Bleichenbacher bit-by-bit oracle attack from partial message knowledge
summary: Oracle attacks show the importance of a correct implementation of cryptographic standards when translated into code. A notable example is the Bleichenbacher attack on RSA with PKCS#1 v1.5 padding and all the improvements that have been suggested over the decades. This paper shows how an attacker knowing a few least significant bytes of an RSA message can take advantage of a server with an oracle side-channel to decrypt the full message bit by bit. We will consider two oracles that can be tested with chosen ciphertexts: one revealing whether the decrypted message starts with the 00 02 bytes and a second one revealing if the decrypted message is fully PKCS compliant. For an attacker knowing the three least significant bytes of the message, the first oracle provides an attack where one oracle call gives the next least significant bit of the message and the second an attack which requires, with high probability, a small constant number of oracle calls to the oracle, with a constant which depends on the length of the message and the desired probability of success. The attack divides the message bits into two sections, one with the known part and one with the unknown part, and then chooses transformations that will keep the unknown part, except for the last unknown bit, orders of magnitude below the integer coming from the known part. The resulting string either gives a valid padding or not depending on the value of the unknown bit. The attacker can minimize the number of oracle calls at the cost of some local computation. Finally, the same method is adapted to show how it can also be used to extract the few least significant bytes of the message with an increased cost where the main complexity is finding a second valid message with a correct padding starting from the original captured ciphertext.

Paper:
title: Exploring the Power Consumption of ERC-4337 Bundling on Server Infrastructure
summary: The Ethereum ecosystem offers the most widespread support for Decentralised Applications (DApps), with over 120 networks currently documented as using variants of the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) for core execution logic. The ERC-4337 standard provides convenient access to DApps for users who do not possess the required cryptocurrency or prefer flexible authorisation of DApp actions. The infrastructure for ERC-4337 implementation can be deployed on any EVM network. However, to aggregate user requests and submit them to the EVM network, ERC-4337 requires operating a bundler, an additional component. Recently, the potential use of ERC-4337 was boosted by another standard, EIP-7702, which can enable ERC-4337 utility for any existing user account. However, the use of the combined EIP-7702/ERC-4337 pattern remains considerably low at less than 6% of EIP-7702 activity. We believe that this underutilisation is at least partly caused by the low number of existing bundling services and their popularity, currently fewer than 15 publicly documented. Expanding the number of bundler nodes would benefit the ecosystem but would introduce operational costs, part of which is represented by the added nodes' power consumption. In this paper, we provide a thorough view of the bundling power consumption aspect using server-grade infrastructure, evaluating both CPU and RAM consumption, as well as the overhead of container-based deployments specific to production environments.

Paper:
title: TileCache: Serving Multi-Round Diffusion Image Editing with Compressed Activation Caches
summary: Multi-round diffusion image editing can reduce computation by reusing intermediate activations, but retaining these activations across editing rounds introduces substantial memory and bandwidth overheads. Compression can reduce these overheads, but efficient cache construction is challenging: compressing only after editing requires buffering over 100 GB of activations per request. Moreover, the compressed cache must support selective reuse, as future masked edits require only a subset of the cached activations. It also exposes a scheduling challenge, as cached edits are faster than initial generations, causing naive policies to severely delay either initial generations or editing requests. In this paper, we aim to address both challenges through compression-informed serving. We develop TileCache, a serving system for multi-round diffusion editing. It compresses reusable activations and incorporates a scheduler that balances both edits and initial generation requests. Compared with the state-of-the-art image editing baseline, TileCache sustains over 2x the request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment. Paper:
title: Understanding Users' Security, Privacy, and Trust Concerns in Healthcare AI Systems
summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into healthcare systems, from clinical information retrieval to workflow automation and decision support, which introduces new security, privacy, and trust risks with direct implications for patient care. While prior work has examined these risks from technical and regulatory perspectives, less is known about how these risks are naturally discussed in online communities. To address this gap, we conduct a large-scale analysis of 14 medical communities on Reddit and extract 6,514 relevant posts. Through systematic qualitative coding and LLM-assisted classification, we investigate concerns expressed in healthcare AI discussions, their prevalence, and how they evolve over time. Our analysis reveals that users perceive healthcare AI as expanding traditional healthcare trust boundaries and attack surfaces through integrations with electronic health records, third-party services, cloud platforms, and automated clinical workflows. Posts express concerns about over-privileged access to sensitive records, opaque data flows, unauthorized secondary use, and unsafe automation can amplify the consequences of errors and misuse. We identify four attitudes toward these risks: exploring questions of accountability and harm, cautiously accepting AI with stronger safeguards, skepticism about system trustworthiness, and resignation to growing data exposure and automation. Longitudinal analysis shows that SP&T discussions have increased significantly, with shifts coinciding with major healthcare AI deployments, privacy incidents, and regulatory developments. These findings illuminate changing trust relationships and data-governance challenges, informing the design and governance of safer, more transparent, and accountable healthcare AI systems.

Paper:
title: eIRWR: Enhanced Iterative Random Walk with Restart for Scalable Root Cause Analysis in Microservices
summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) in microservice systems must find the faulty service behind symptoms that spread across hundreds or thousands of dependent services. Graph-based random walk methods propagate anomaly evidence over the service dependency graph. However, existing anomaly-restart walks restart from the raw anomaly vector, which is often dominated by strongly anomalous downstream victims rather than the less anomalous source. Through a controlled ablation of a basic anomaly-restart walk, the Iterative Random Walk with Restart (IRWR), we show that its ``resilience damping'' is equivalent to a higher restart probability in Personalized PageRank (PPR). Basic IRWR is therefore no stronger than a restart-tuned PPR, which we adopt as a fairer baseline. We then present Enhanced IRWR (eIRWR), which goes beyond restart tuning. It (a)~concentrates restart mass on the most suspicious nodes through power-law sharpening and (b)~adds self-loops and backward edges so that probability accumulates at cascade sources. On three large topologies (12K--25K nodes) from the Alibaba Microservice Trace Dataset, eIRWR is the most accurate of the compared graph-based methods at every level of root-cause visibility. At visibility $v = 0.3$, it reaches a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of $0.78$, about four times a restart-tuned PPR and nine times the best other baseline. At high visibility, it reaches MRR\,$= 0.95$ and runs in under 30\,ms on graphs with 17K nodes, so it is suitable for online use.

Paper:
title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems
summary: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams

Paper:
title: RAS: Measuring LLM Safety Through Refusal Alignment
summary: Repeated safety evaluation of open-weight large language models requires generating and judging responses for many related checkpoints. We introduce RAS (Refusal Alignment Score), a representation-based, reference-relative indicator of harmful-request refusal computed by the five-stage SafeVec procedure. SafeVec extracts layer-wise refusal directions from an aligned reference model, measures their alignment in related targets, and calibrates a score from 0 to 100 using behavioral attack success rates (ASR) from reference and calibration models. Subsequent target scoring uses input forward passes alone. Across 18 held-out variants from the Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, RAS correlates with $100(1-\mathrm{ASR})$ (Pearson 0.934, Spearman 0.851) and achieves 83.0% pairwise ordering agreement. Across five prompt configurations for the Llama reference, directions have mean cosine similarity 0.939. With calibration ASR already available, setup-inclusive evaluation of five targets achieves a speedup of 3.2 to 80.5 times over the specified behavioral protocol. These results support refusal alignment as an efficient signal for screening related checkpoints and prioritizing behavioral audits.

Paper:
title: Sequential Semantic-Non-Semantic Watermarking: Robustness Against UnMarker Attacks
summary: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated digital content generation and intensified concerns around fraud, misuse, counterfeiting, and content provenance. Defensive image watermarking provides a practical mechanism for identifying and tracing digital content, but recent watermark-removal attacks challenge its robustness. This study investigates Sequential Semantic Non-Semantic Watermarking (SSNSW), which combines HiDDeN and StegaStamp as complementary non-semantic and semantic watermarking schemes. Using 50 images from MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ, both embedding orders are evaluated, followed by UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks applied individually and sequentially.
  Results show that both watermarks remain highly decodable after dual embedding, with only limited embedding-order effects. Under individual attacks, one watermark generally remains strongly decodable: StegaStamp under the non-semantic attack and HiDDeN under the semantic attack. Sequential attacks are therefore required to substantially reduce both watermark signals, while attack order has a limited and configuration-dependent effect. The semantic attack also shows a broader effect across the two watermark types than the non-semantic attack. LPIPS remains relatively low in several settings, although qualitative inspection reveals noticeable distortions, particularly in selected facial images, indicating that LPIPS should not be used alone to assess visual quality.
  Overall, the findings show that combining complementary watermark types can increase robustness against single-stage removal attacks and motivate broader multi-layer watermarking, stronger perceptual evaluation, and further study of sequential watermark-removal strategies.

Paper:
title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-based Management of Continuum Resources
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/lilanpei/continuum-intent-compiler.

Paper:
title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
summary: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.

Paper:
title: NL-SME: Enhancing Multi-Step Gradient Inversion through Adaptive Two-State Matching
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training among multiple clients without directly sharing their raw data.However, gradient inversion attacks can exploit the model updates exchanged during training to reconstruct clients' private data.With multiple local training steps, an observed update combines gradients evaluated at changing model states and potentially different mini-batches, while intermediate states remain hidden. Restricting gradient evaluation to a single state on the segment between the initial and final models can exclude states that better fit the accumulated update.We consider reconstruction from an individual client's endpoint models, assuming that the training labels are known.We propose NL-SME, a regularized two-state gradient surrogate for matching multi-step client updates without replaying local training.The surrogate adapts its evaluation center, regularizes its displacement, and averages raw parameter gradients at two shared symmetric states.We evaluate NL-SME against existing gradient inversion methods on FEMNIST and CIFAR-100 with varying numbers of local training steps.The results show improved reconstruction quality, highlighting the privacy risks of sharing individual client updates after multiple local steps.

Paper:
title: Security of Deep Research Agents: Attack Surface, Defenses, Benchmarks, and Agenda Seeding against Research Planning
summary: Deep research and agentic search agents autonomously retrieve content from the open web and generate reports with citations, and their outputs are often taken directly as research conclusions. This paper systematizes security research in this area along four stages, namely retrieval, planning, evidence integration, and report generation. We present a unified threat model, a taxonomy of attacks and defenses, and a review of evaluation benchmarks, and we align the area dimension by dimension with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization (GEO). Coding 34 primary studies shows that only 26.5% of them involve the planning stage, and none performs an end-to-end poisoning evaluation on commercial products. To address this gap, we propose the agenda seeding attack, in which the attacker writes no instructions and only introduces a fictitious evaluation metric. Across 3,520 sandboxed research runs under the same budget, GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, whereas agenda seeding makes the attacker's target the top pick in 16% to 28% of reports. Injection detection and query anchoring fail against it, verification prompting hurts utility, and our proposed provenance tagging preserves utility but can be bypassed by multi-site bait. Finally, we propose eight research directions.

Paper:
title: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections
summary: Prompt injection is the most critical vulnerability in deployed AI agents. Despite recent progress, we show that the prevailing defense paradigm (data-instruction separation) both fails to detect attacks that operate through contextual manipulation and degrades contextually appropriate behavior. We then recast prompt injection via the lens of Contextual Integrity (CI), a privacy theory that judges information flow compliance with contextual norms. This explains types of attacks that current defenses attempt to patch and predict advanced ones future agents will face. We develop unique benign and attack scenarios that force an agent to violate the norms by (1) misrepresenting the flow, (2) manipulating norms, or (3) mixing multiple flows. This reframing suggests an impossibility argument: an adversary can always construct a context under which a blocked flow appears legitimate, or a defender who tightens norms will block genuinely legitimate flows. Our findings suggest that current research addresses a shrinking fraction of future attack surfaces. Instead, through CI, we offer a principled framework for evaluating context-sensitive failures, and designing CI-aware alignment for frontier autonomous agents.

Paper:
title: Two-Robot Evacuation from a Unit Disk in the Segment Visibility Model
summary: Under segment visibility, two robots discover a target as soon as it belongs to the segment joining their positions, even if neither robot has physically reached it. We study two unit-speed robots starting at the center of a unit disk that must both reach an exit (target) placed at an unknown point of its boundary. In our model robots are permitted to leave the disk while searching. We give a three-phase tangent-and-arc algorithm whose exact worst-case evacuation time is 2\sqrt{3}+π/3 \approx 4.511299$. We also prove a matching lower bound for the class of descending horizontal full-slice sweeps, allowing asymmetric robot trajectories. The proof uses an exterior path-length inequality and a feasible minimum-half-width symmetrization. Determining the optimal time over all segment-visibility algorithms remains open.

Paper:
title: Vectorised Hashing Based on Bernstein-Rabin-Winograd Polynomials over Prime Order Fields
summary: We introduce the new AXU hash function decBRWHash, which is parameterised by the positive integer $c$ and is based on Bernstein-Rabin-Winograd (BRW) polynomials. Choosing $c>1$ gives a hash function which can be implemented using $c$-way single instruction multiple data (SIMD) instructions. We report a set of very comprehensive hand optimised assembly implementations of 4-decBRWHash using avx2 SIMD instructions available on modern Intel processors. For comparison, we also report similar carefully optimised avx2 assembly implementations of polyHash, an AXU hash function based on usual polynomials. Our implementations are over prime order fields, specifically the primes $2^{127}-1$ and $2^{130}-5$. For the prime $2^{130}-5$, for avx2 implementations, compared to the famous Poly1305 hash function, 4-decBRWHash is faster for messages which are a few hundred bytes long and achieves a speed-up of about 16% for message lengths in a few kilobytes range and improves to a speed-up of about 23% for message lengths in a few megabytes range.

Paper:
title: Could Mobile AI be Exploited?: Understanding the Exploitations of Trust and Ethics Gap in On-Device Small Language Models
summary: In this paper, we present a very first study to investigate trust and ethical implications of on-device artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on small language models (SLMs) amenable for personal devices like smartphones. While on-device SLMs promise enhanced privacy, reduced latency, and improved user experience compared to cloud-based services, we posit that they might also introduce significant risks and vulnerabilities compared to their on-server counterparts. As part of our study, we conduct a systematic evaluation of the state-of-the-art on-devices SLMs, compared to their on-server counterparts, using well-established trust and ethics frameworks. Our results illustrate that on-device SLMs are significantly less trustworthy and lacks ethical safeguards, specifically demonstrating more stereotypical, unfair, privacy-breaching and harmful content generation behavior. Further, these risks of on-device SLMs could be exploited through Open Knowledge (OkNow) Attacks, and we demonstrated them using potentially unethical vanilla prompts, to which the on-device SLMs answer with valid responses without any filters and without the need for any jailbreaking or prompt engineering. These responses can be abused for various harmful and unethical scenarios like: societal harm, illegal activities, hate, self-harm, exploitable phishing content, disinformation and many others.

Paper:
title: CHERI under Fault Injection: An Emulation-Based Security Evaluation of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions
summary: Memory-safety vulnerabilities continue to dominate real-world exploit chains despite decades of research into software mitigations. CHERI is a hardware architecture that enforces spatial and temporal memory safety by augmenting pointers with hardware-checked metadata, thus preventing software-based exploitation, but its threat model explicitly excludes fault injection. This thesis investigates whether targeted fault injection can undermine CHERI's memory-safety guarantees in a pure-capability CHERI-RISC-V environment. Two fault classes are considered: bit flips corrupting capability metadata, and fault-induced check skipping on capability store instructions.
  We implement fault injection primitives in a QEMU-based emulation environment, which enables deterministic, repeatable experiments without specialised hardware. With them, we demonstrate four attack scenarios: buffer overflows, control-flow hijacking, data-only attacks, and use-after-free. Each succeeds with one or two targeted faults (lower bounds under the emulation-based setting). Check skipping offers an alternative route to control-flow hijacking and data-only attacks, with a minimum of one fault.
  These results show that CHERI's guarantees depend on the physical integrity of capability metadata, the uninterrupted execution of metadata checks, and the integrity of the revocation bitmap: a single targeted fault can circumvent spatial safety, temporal safety, or control-flow integrity. CHERI still raises the cost of exploitation, since fault injection is a prerequisite for every attack and the sentry mechanism forces an attacker to supply a valid tagged capability or spend a second fault restoring the tag. Based on these findings, we propose mitigations: ECC-protected capability memory, capability field authentication codes, redundant execution of security-critical checks, and revocation bitmap integrity verification.

Paper:
title: Recovery Gone Too Far: Understanding and Repairing Risky Fallback in LLM Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through tools, reading repositories, running builds, and pushing code. When a tool fails with an ordinary error, such as a rate limit or a timeout, the agent can fall back to a substitute tool and still complete the task. However, the same fallback that completes a task in one environment can cross an action boundary in another. For example, after a push is rejected, a forced push in one repository replaces only the agent's own commits, while in a different repository it also removes another author's commits. We call such a fallback a risky fallback. To understand this phenomenon, we conduct an empirical study on 304 scenarios that span eight domains and cover 55 real CVEs. All four mainstream models we evaluate exhibit risky fallback, with action-boundary violations in up to 96.8% of risky scenarios. We further evaluate three mainstream mitigations and find that none of them is effective against risky fallback. We then present nrepair. At each call to the substitute tool, nrepair scores the agent's context with a monitor whose threshold is calibrated on normal runs alone; when the monitor triggers, it withholds the call once and returns the decision to the agent. nrepair reduces action-boundary violations on all four models, by up to 76.0% (from 67.5% to 16.2%), at a negligible runtime cost. On most models, the normal success rate drops by less than 7%. We also evaluate nrepair on two production agents, Claude Code and Codex, and find that it is equally effective on both.

Paper:
title: Suppression Is Not Erasure: Mechanistic Analysis and Reactivation Boundaries of Subspace Projection for LoRA Backdoor Defense
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used to customize large language models, but third-party adapters create supply-chain backdoor risks with under 1% modified parameters. Recent analytical null-space and subspace projection defenses report near-zero static Attack Success Rates (ASR), equating static silence with erasure. We audit subspace-projection defenses across four scales (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B), three architectures (Qwen2.5, InternLM2.5-1.8B, Spark-X2.6-4B), and five trigger families (suffix, natural phrase, prefix/in-sentence, double-negation syntax, and composite triggers). Statically, module-wise rank-1 trigger-difference projection cuts ASR from 60.4% to 0.0% on standard suites and 70.3% to 0.0% on 1,000 uncontaminated prompts (p = 3.055e-299) in under 5 s. By Theorem 1 (11,880/11,880 module-sample pairs), low-rank bottleneck amplification aligns benign polite-suffix probes with u_1(B) (median cosine 0.8934-0.9705), reaching 0.0% ASR without trigger knowledge. However, static suppression is not erasure. Under 5-sample reactivation, single-round weight-editing baselines rebound to 91.7%-100.0% ASR in Epoch 1 (Fine-Pruning, ANP, NEEDLE, LoRA-Patch; 48.7% for single-round dual projection) and 100.0% by Epoch 2. Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 prove single-sided projection leaves non-zero gradients along u_1 across 168/168 modules (27.2x-31.1x above random expectation), while Haar orthogonal rotation shows Epoch-2 immunity depends on semantic alignment rather than Frobenius norm. Guided by Theorems 1-2, we propose Single-Shot Rank-k Dual-Subspace Erasure (DSE) and Benign Subspace Anchoring (DSE-BA), achieving 0.0% static ASR and 0.0% Epoch-1 reactivation across all five trigger families and Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B, while cutting Epoch-2 ASR to 25.0% (43.33% +/- 2.49% on 50 prompts x 3 seeds) and benign PPL to 6.54.

Paper:
title: HalluProbe: Exploiting VLM Hallucinations for Backdoor Detection
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks introduced through data poisoning, making effective backdoor detection a critical security challenge. In this paper, we uncover a novel connection between VLM hallucinations and backdoor behaviors and exploit this connection for backdoor detection. Our key insight is that poisoned training data induces strong language priors toward the backdoor target token, while such priors are also a major source of hallucinations. This suggests that enhancing hallucinations can expose hidden backdoor-related priors. Specifically, backdoored VLMs tend to hallucinate backdoor target tokens more frequently across diverse inputs, while the hallucinated tokens of clean VLMs are largely random and exhibit no stable target-specific bias. Based on this observation, we propose HalluProbe, which enhances hallucinations during output decoding and measures the distributional consistency of hallucinated tokens to identify backdoored VLMs. We evaluate HalluProbe against six representative VLM backdoor attacks across three models. Experimental results demonstrate that HalluProbe can effectively detect backdoored VLMs with an accuracy exceeding 90%, outperforming existing backdoor detection methods.

Paper:
title: Local Order Matters: A Lightweight CPU-Trainable CNN for Website Fingerprinting on Defended Tor Traffic
summary: Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks let a passive adversary infer which site a Tor user visits from the encrypted cell sequence. On undefended traffic, hand-crafted-feature attacks are already near-ceiling, so deep learning offers only a marginal advantage there. We show that the decisive regime is defended traffic: against the FRONT padding defense, which injects dummy cells that corrupt the volume and count features feature attacks rely on, a compact 95,103-parameter 1-D convolutional network trained on the raw cell-direction sequence, on CPU only, stays robust while three implemented direction-only feature baselines degrade. On the closed-world WFlib FRONT set (95 sites), our model reaches 54.2% top-1 accuracy versus 38.5% for the strongest implemented feature baseline (k-FP-style RF), a gain of 15.7 percentage points (3 seeds; seed-0 paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+14.5, +17.0] pp on per-trace correctness, excluding zero). On undefended traffic the CNN reaches 94.1% versus 92.3% for k-FP-style RF. A controlled order-ablation permutes only nonzero traffic cells within each trace, preserving direction counts, retained length, and trailing zero-padding positions while destroying traffic order. This collapses the CNN below every feature baseline (from 54.2% to 7.6%, a 46.6 pp drop), showing that the model depends strongly on order-derived information under FRONT.

Paper:
title: LiteLMGuard: Seamless and Lightweight On-Device Guardrails for Small Language Models against Quantization Vulnerabilities
summary: The growing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has influenced the development of Small Language Models (SLMs) for on-device deployment across smartphones and edge devices, offering enhanced privacy, reduced latency, server-free functionality, and improved user experience. However, due to on-device resource constraints, SLMs undergo size optimization through compression techniques like quantization, which inadvertently introduce fairness, ethical and privacy risks. Critically, quantized SLMs may respond to harmful queries directly, without requiring adversarial manipulation, raising significant safety and trust concerns. To address this, we propose LiteLMGuard, an on-device guardrail that provides real-time, prompt-level defense for quantized SLMs. Additionally, our guardrail is designed to be model-agnostic such that it can be seamlessly integrated with any SLM, operating independently of underlying architectures. Our LiteLMGuard formalizes deep learning (DL)-based prompt filtering by leveraging semantic understanding to classify prompt answerability for SLMs. Built on our curated Answerable-or-Not dataset, LiteLMGuard employs ELECTRA as the candidate model with 97.75% answerability classification accuracy. The on-device deployment of LiteLMGuard enabled real-time offline filtering with over 85% defense-rate against harmful prompts (including jailbreak attacks), 94% filtering accuracy and ~135 ms average latency. These results demonstrate LiteLMGuard as a lightweight robust defense mechanism for effectively and efficiently securing on-device SLMs against Open Knowledge Attacks.

Paper:
title: Seamless Reconfiguration for DAG-BFT (Technical Report)
summary: Byzantine Atomic Broadcast in Asynchronous networks has been studied extensively for decades. In a fully asynchronous system with even one possible crash failure, the FLP impossibility result rules out deterministic consensus, motivating randomized protocols that achieve termination with probability one. More recently, DAG-Rider popularized a new abstraction in which processes continuously reliably broadcast blocks to construct a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and then locally derive a total order using a randomized perfect coin. This separation of dissemination from ordering has renewed interest in asynchronous DAG-based Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) and inspired numerous protocols that improve expected latency or throughput. Reconfiguration, however, remains largely unexplored. Existing DAG-based BFT protocols generally assume a static set of processes, whereas deployed systems must occasionally add or remove nodes in response to operational demands. Existing solutions are not seamless; they either pause the system or delay membership changes until a predetermined epoch boundary. This may be impractical and can introduce downtime. A single agreed switching round is difficult to use seamlessly: by the time processes learn it, the dissemination layer may already have advanced beyond it. In this work, we present a seamless reconfiguration protocol for Asynchronous DAG-based Byzantine Atomic Broadcast. Our protocol allows the DAG to continue growing while the membership and corresponding quorum thresholds change, without halting the system. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first protocol to provide seamless reconfiguration for DAG-based Byzantine atomic broadcast in a fully asynchronous network.

Paper:
title: Where Is Rank-1 DiM Refusal Intervenable in Multimodal LM Derivatives?
summary: Open-weight model hubs now ship not only chat checkpoints but a long tail of derivatives---fine-tunes, safety guards, vision--language models (VLMs), audio wrappers, and generative heads---yet residual-stream safety audits still often intervene at a single site, usually the text decoder $T$. We ask a localization question under one shared mean / rank-1 difference-in-means (DiM) extract$=$intervene protocol, with matched-norm random and empty-rate controls: does causal chat attack lift concentrate at $T$, or do perceptual encoders, projectors, and fusion paths ($E$/$P$/$F$) supply a comparable bypass? On the mixed-input settings we stress-test---HADES adversarial images paired with harmful text prompts, and spoken AdvBench via text-to-speech (TTS) or silence---text DiM at $T$ raises attack success rate (ASR) while the same mean DiM at $E$/$P$/$F$ does not; attacks track harmful text rather than image or audio content. Margin-rank and leverage probes on a Vision leaf show that this recipe is extremal at $T$ and near chance at $P$/$E$, which pressures a weak-extractor reading of those flat cells for the DiM family we study. Catalog breadth and mapper-free base$\to$derivative transfer when residual widths match provide supporting coverage under the same gates; generative U-Nets are a separate band under generation judges. The primary claim is this recipe-scoped $T$ vs.\ non-text intervenability asymmetry---intervention accessibility under mean / rank-1 DiM, not a claim that refusal is absent or fully represented outside $T$ (text vs.\ perceptual contrasts and pooling differ by site). On VLGuard Unsafe prompts ($n{=}200$; Llama-Guard), the same $T$ vs.\ $P$/$E$ directionality holds at modest absolute ASR ($0.030{\to}0.150$ at $T$). An intervention-oriented Class$\times$site ledger records where this protocol still hooks as supporting coverage, not as a universal multimodal bypass.

Paper:
title: BitBypass: A New Direction in Jailbreaking Aligned Large Language Models with Bitstream Camouflage
summary: The inherent risk of generating harmful and unsafe content by Large Language Models (LLMs), has highlighted the need for their safety alignment. Various techniques like supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and red-teaming were developed for ensuring the safety alignment of LLMs. However, the robustness of these aligned LLMs is always challenged by adversarial attacks that exploit unexplored and underlying vulnerabilities of the safety alignment. In this paper, we develop a novel black-box jailbreak attack, called BitBypass, that leverages hyphen-separated bitstream camouflage for jailbreaking aligned LLMs. This represents a new direction in jailbreaking by exploiting fundamental information representation of data as continuous bits, rather than leveraging prompt engineering or adversarial manipulations. Our evaluation of five state-of-the-art LLMs, namely GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3.5, Llama 3.1, and Mixtral, in adversarial perspective, revealed the capabilities of BitBypass in bypassing their safety alignment and tricking them into generating harmful and unsafe content. Further, we observed that BitBypass outperforms several state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks in terms of stealthiness and attack success. Overall, these results highlights the effectiveness and efficiency of BitBypass in jailbreaking these state-of-the-art LLMs.

Paper:
title: Membership Inference Attacks on Recommender System: A Survey
summary: Recommender systems (RecSys) have been widely applied across e-commerce, finance, healthcare, and social media and have become increasingly influential in shaping user behavior and decision-making, underscoring their growing impact across domains. Since RecSys heavily relies on user data, its privacy concerns are significant and need to be addressed urgently. Recent studies on membership inference attacks (MIAs) in RecSys highlight this need. MIAs aim to infer whether a user or an interaction record was used to train a target RecSys model. Successful MIAs can lead to severe privacy breaches, such as revealing sensitive aspects of users' lifestyles. MIAs in RecSys have features distinct from those targeting classification models or large language models. However, no systematic survey on this topic has yet been conducted. We present the first comprehensive survey on RecSys MIAs, exploring their taxonomy, design principles, evaluation methods, and defense mechanisms. Based on the summary of existing studies in this area, we also outline several promising future research directions. This survey aims to raise awareness of privacy risks among RecSys researchers, practitioners, and users, and promote privacy protection practices in RecSys design.

Paper:
title: When Backdoors Can Be Switched Off: Suppression-Aware Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations, robot states, and natural-language instructions to robotic actions, but their multimodal interfaces introduce new security risks. Existing VLA backdoor attacks primarily study trigger-based activation and stealthy action manipulation, leaving conditional suppression of malicious behavior underexplored. We investigate suppression-aware backdoors, which combine conjunctive trigger activation with instruction-conditioned suppression. We instantiate this design through three variants: Cross-Modal Trigger, combining robot-state and spatially separated visual triggers; Self-Suppressing Trigger, requiring a state trigger and a [DISRUPT] instruction token for activation, with [RESTORE] token suppressing the attack; and Multi-Trigger, additionally requiring a visual trigger while retaining suppression even when physical triggers persist. We evaluate these attacks using SmolVLA on two SO-100 manipulation datasets against four baselines: State Backdoor, BadVLA, TabVLA, and SilentDrift. Self-Suppressing and Multi-Trigger reduce Isolation Forest detection from 96--98% to 1--18% and action-space l divergence by 10--14X, achieving 63--71% attack success rates with perfect clean-task performance. Experiments with OpenVLA on LIBERO further show that the attacks transfer to a 7B-parameter policy, evading STRIP and action-distribution-shift detection. Our findings establish conditional suppression as an important dimension for evaluating backdoor threats in VLA policies.

Paper:
title: Compositional Exploits in Autonomous Coding Agents: Attack Mechanics and Ephemeral Defense
summary: Autonomous coding agents (such as Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenHands) rely on third-party tools to inspect files, run commands, and call external APIs. Today's security auditors evaluate these tools almost entirely in isolation: static linters and AST checkers verify that each individual tool contains no malicious code at installation time. In this paper, we show that isolated tool auditing is fundamentally flawed. We expose compositional exploits in autonomous coding agents, an emergent vulnerability class where an agent chains individually harmless tools to execute an unauthorized attack. Much like code-reuse attacks in binary exploitation, this threat requires no malware; instead, the agent stitches together legitimate tool operations across turns over shared workspace files, environment variables, and chat memory. Across a 560-task benchmark suite (360 exploit tasks across 8 hazard classes and 200 benign developer and cloud workflows), unprotected frontier models (Gemini 3.5, 3.7, and 3.8 Flash) execute compositional exploit chains with a 72.9% to 84.5% success rate, while five leading single-tool pre-distribution scanners exhibit a 0% detection rate across all constituent tools. To eliminate compositional exploits, we present CompGuard, an OS-grounded defense uniting two planes: (1) a Cognitive Control Plane that issues single-skill capability leases and tracks dataflow provenance, and (2) an OS Kernel Enforcement Layer using Linux Landlock LSM v4, seccomp-BPF socket filters, and an ephemeral loopback proxy to close the invocation gap. CompGuard achieves a 100% Defense Block Rate (0.0% to 0.8% pre-teardown Net ASR) at 61.4 microseconds interposition overhead, preserves a 98.0% solve rate on benign developer workflows, and triggers zero false alarms across 615 real cloud diagnostic calls.

Paper:
title: Speeding up Automated Algorithm Design by Batch Evaluation: A Case Study of Genetic Programming for Ant Colony Optimisation
summary: Evaluation is becoming the bottleneck of automated algorithm design, especially for iterative algorithms such as ant colony optimisation (ACO), which must run to completion on multiple instances. Paper:
title: BrownoutMoE: Learning Structure-Aware Expert Grouping for Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts Model Serving
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models (LLMs) are increasingly served on multi-GPU clusters in cloud data centers, where inference must stay accurate and responsive under bursty demand. Expert access in MoE inference is highly imbalanced: a few hot experts process most tokens, whereas many cold experts fragment kernels and leave GPU parallelism underused. Paper:
title: A Maximum Entropy Implementation of Differential Privacy Under Linear Invariants
summary: Differential privacy is the standard for ensuring data privacy and is widely used in major data publications, including reporting results from the U.S. decennial census. Common implementation of differential privacy uses independent Gaussian or Laplace noise addition to the database. However, there could be aggregate (linear) queries to the database that are excluded from the privacy budget, for example, state totals that can not be perturbed due to constitutional mandates. Any implementation of a differential privacy is required to honor these constraints, also referred to as invariants. Under aggregation constraints, the noise vector is no longer independent and the traditional differential privacy guarantees have to be re-evaluated. We propose a high entropy differential privacy implementation that maintains the aggregation invariants with probability one or exponentially close to one and derive the privacy guarantees for the implementation under the invariants. The theoretical proof also gives a solution to an open question about the null space of correlation matrices. Moreover, the methodology has general use in the context of sampling from normal mixture models under linear equality constraints.

Paper:
title: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
summary: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.

summary: This paper proposes a new decentralized framework, named EDGChain-E (Encrypted-Data-Git Chain for Energy), designed to manage version-controlled, encrypted energy data using blockchain and the InterPlanetary File System. Paper:
title: ExclaveFL: Verifiable Claims for Federated Learning using Exclaves
summary: In federated learning (FL), data providers jointly train a machine learning model without sharing training data. This makes it challenging to provide verifiable claims about the trained model, e.g., related to the employed training data, data sanitization, or training algorithm---a malicious data provider can simply deviate from the correct training protocol without detection. Prior FL training systems have used trusted execution environments (TEEs) to protect the training computation, relying on the confidentiality and integrity of TEEs. TEE confidentiality, however, has been shown to be vulnerable to various attacks, e.g., via side channels.
  We describe ExclaveFL, a system for training FL models that establishes verifiable claims about models through fine-grained runtime attestation proofs. Since such proofs only require integrity, ExclaveFL generates them using exclaves, which are integrity-only execution environments without software-managed secrets, making them immune to data leakage attacks. ExclaveFL uses exclaves to attest data transformations during FL training, and the runtime attestation proofs then form an attested dataflow graph of the entire training computation. The graph is checked by an auditor to ensure that the trained model satisfies claims, e.g., about the use of data sanitization by data providers or aggregation by the model provider. Since exclaves require minor yet proprietary firmware changes, we evaluate a variant with similar performance but slightly weaker security guarantees on existing AMD SEV-SNP hardware. We show that ExclaveFL introduces less than 12% overhead compared to unprotected FL model training.

Paper:
title: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
summary: With the ever-increasing parameter scale and structural complexity of deep neural network (DNN) models, traditional cloud-based inference encounters bottlenecks in performance, privacy protection, and energy efficiency. While edge computing and edge intelligence facilitate the migration of inference tasks to edge servers closer to the data source, existing end-edge-cloud collaborative inference still encounters critical challenges, such as sensitivity to heterogeneous resources, complexity in multi-objective optimization, and adaptability to dynamic workloads. To achieve the joint optimization of end-to-end latency and energy consumption under dynamic inference requests with multi-resource constraints, we propose IA-MoE, an intensity-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework. By modeling the model partitioning problem as a bilateral matching problem between layer tasks and virtual machine resources for each inference request, IA-MoE dynamically partitions DNN models in an edge-cloud hybrid computing environment. We evaluate IA-MoE using three representative DNNs (i.e., AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet50) on two public inference datasets in an enhanced CloudSimSDN simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that IA-MoE outperforms baseline methods regarding weighted normalized metrics for end-to-end latency and energy consumption. To our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce the MoE paradigm for DNN partitioning and collaborative inference in hybrid computing environments, providing a practical solution for efficient inference in artificial intelligence applications.

Paper:
title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
summary: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of a claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks normalization and makes algorithmic conversion non-transitive.
  We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($irrel : ΠP{:}Prop.\,Πp,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, $Π$-covariant subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, compile to unification-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$), and match declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) for open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.
